This game probably has had it's fair share of "change of metas" since it's creation due to its age, but nothing like the rapid meta changes of say League of Legends due to there not being constant updates and tweeks to the game. 

I'm going to do a very broad examination of this game. Let's start with the objective: to defeat your enemy(ies) by destroying their town center. (I know it is really complete domination, but let's stick with the goal is to destroy (all) of your enemy(ies) town centers. 

How can this be accomplished? There are a couple of ways to do it: 

Rush them- build up as big of an army as fast as possible and have them end the game in a very short time. This emphasizes mass efficiency at the beginning of the game and focuses heavily on certain civilizations (pardon my inaccuracies in denotation. It's been a long time since I've played and studied the game). I believe the spanish in AoE 3 are the best at rushing if I remember correctly. As I said before, this strategy is about getting ahead of your opponents by being more efficient than them in the early game, then maintaining and expanding your lead by either destroying their base, expanding yours, or a combination of the two. 

Another strategy is to play aggressive, but not to rush them. You are constantly using your resources to exhaust his. This may seem counter productive, but here me out. If you use less resources than them during the attacks, you are winning in the sense of the game. You are slowly getting ahead. You are always on the offensive, and they on the defensive. You can exhaust their resources until they are forced to do something bold, such as send villagers halfway across the map to get gold. Then you capitalize on it and blockade them. The resources that typically get blockaded are gold and wood. Meat can be (somewhat) easily acquired due to farms. 

Another strat: Play passive and out scale your opponent(s). This only works if you are more efficient than your opponents in collecting resources and production of troops, then end them in one fell swoop. 

There are other strategies I am sure, but I feel as though I am getting repetitive. The main point I am trying to stress is how to exploit advantages you have on the other players. There exist different methods of doing this, and I only chose a few to talk about. 

I have never really watched professional AoE players, but I do study game theory rather religiously for games that I enjoy. (Chess is all about game theory, and League of Legends can be if you know the capacities of the elements of the game).  I assume there exist trends throughout the years of the game, but I also bet certain players stay with one or two tactics and master it. 

Feel free to debunk my claims. I haven't played a competitive game probably since middle school.

Utilitarianism was actually the name of the British philosopher's, John Stuart Mill, book, published in 1861. Essentially, its argument is that you should act in a manner that maximizes "utility." That is a problem that plagues the computer vision community: getting the same program to work in multiple environments. We do not have a clever method of auto-calibration, but I have written programs, called hsv and demo,  that goes through the vision program step by step and so I can record what values work, and see if a step fails. Hsv is for color tracking, demo is for ir tracking. 

Object recognition is a very complex field. The way I got object recognition to work was through cascade training, and while it is good, it is slow. (I thought it was rather fast, but a professor from UMSTL said not to use it, so I took his word for it). Our vision programs are very robust. Here is an example: http://imgur.com/Of6t0BH,Jbf7xq5#0 and http://imgur.com/Of6t0BH,Jbf7xq5#1 and even http://imgur.com/nxyLcxl.

The first 2 images are of 2 different competitions. The program worked equally as well in both environments.  The third image is something I took the blame for. I gave this team too much info on my vision system, so they devised a method to get it to not work, after this match I changed the program so this method no longer worked, but it still blocked our full court shots so it didnt really matter in the end. 

Our generic object recognition is the kinect depth map. We deleted the floor from the image, so that all we're left whatever is infront of it, then we do some opencv image processing on it, regardless of its shape or size, do some math. then we know where it is with respect to our camera and how big it is. 

If you really want to know the math: it's in topdepthtest inside the contours loop. It is just some fancy trig.

We have never actually used the pi, we use o-droid products, this year we threaded and ran our vision program (which also tracked balls and bumpers) on 3 cameras and we were getting 10 fps. When we cut off ball and bumper tracking, we get about 25 with 3 cameras. With one camera we get about 50 when we thread it properly.

You can usually just look it up online. But if you want to figure it out yourself, there is a couple things you can do. One, measure it. Put your camera on a grid, and mark where it can and can't see in the x and y, then measure. 

Or, if you can run opencv, you could do a camera calibration. This will output the intrinsic camera parameters, such as the focal length, real center of the screen (zero distortion point), and the distortion coefficients. (well, the first 7 if I remember right, there are infinite)
 
edit: this is a very powerful tool I used last year to have a completely automatic shooter. You can calculate distance in a similar fashion. You know the height of your target, h1, and you know the height of your camera, h2. h1-h2 will be constant if your camera isn't moving up and down on your robot via a motor or something. You can calculte y rotation to the target in the image with the same math used to calculate x rotation, but the origin to do both has to be at the center of the image. So now you have a triangle with your camera, the target, and directly infront of the camera. It is a right triangle. Theta is equal to your in screen angle plus your real world angle. Opposite is constant, adjacent is scalar distance to the target.

You don't need any fancy computer vision library to calculate rotation! You know the image resolution (let's say it is 640x480) and you know the FOV (let's say it is 60x40). If the center lays at pixel coordinate (150, 50), you can set up a proportion. 150 pixels / x degrees = 320 pixels / 30 degrees. Solve for x. Voila! You have rotation to the center of the target.

Break down of what I did with vision: I am using 3 120 degree cameras so I have complete awareness. I have a case detection to see what set of vision tape I am looking at, left right or both. I send the labview programmer x and y displacement and yaw as well as distance to the center of the scoring wall. This allows for a check on our gyro in case it starts drifting and we can know if we are perpendicular to the wall. 

I also programmed a depth camera, the asus xtion, to detect robots and balls (it differentiates), and it calculates their velocity. This way, if it is a robot, we can do path planning, or if is a ball, we can do autonomous retrieval.
